**Summary.** The paper introduces the Hilbert-Killing metric, an emergent quantum geometry derived from generalizing the adiabatic gauge potential. This metric serves as a sensitive diagnostic tool to locate the boundary between integrable and ergodic regimes in many-body quantum systems like the Ising model. Its robust scaling behavior at this phase transition makes it a powerful theoretical signature for studying quantum thermalization.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful geometric tool to diagnose thermalization dynamics, which is crucial for understanding quantum chaos and non-equilibrium steady states relevant to AMO physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central challenge is finding universal, robust, and interpretable geometric signatures that mark the precise onset of many-body ergodicity in quantum systems.

**Main result.** The derived Hilbert-Killing (HK) metric successfully probes this boundary, showing its maximum response precisely where the system transitions between integrable and ergodic regimes for both Ising and PXP models.

**Method.** The authors generalize the adiabatic gauge potential to multi-parameter perturbations, constructing the HK metric tensor which quantifies total eigenstate variation across parameter space.

**Model / system.** The study uses general quantum many-body systems, specifically analyzing the spin-1/2 one-dimensional mixed field Ising model and a constrained PXP model, parameterized by external fields ($h_x, h_z$).

**Key observables.** Hilbert-Killing (HK) metric components ($G_{\mu
u}$), spectrum-averaged variance of the AGP ($\sigma^2_{A_\mu}$), and the Casimir invariant ($\Omega$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The system parameters defining the Hamiltonian, particularly investigating the crossover region between integrable and ergodic limits.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Previous metrics are often ill-behaved near the boundary; the HK metric is proposed to overcome this by providing a comprehensive geometric measure.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the concept of the HK metric defining geometry in parameter space, showing maximum scaling response at the ergodic/integrable phase boundary for both Ising and PXP models.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the HK metric from the adiabatic gauge potential, applies it to analyze the Ising model across different phases (Fig. 1, 2), confirms universality using the PXP model (Fig. 3), and explores deeper connections via entanglement fidelity and Casimir invariants in random matrix models (Fig. 4-8).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Identifying universal, robust, and interpretable signatures of the onset of ergodicity remains a major challenge. The adiabatic gauge potential has been noted to act as a sensitive probe of quantum chaos. In this work, we generalize the features of the adiabatic gauge potential to multi-parameter perturbations, yielding an emergent quantum geometry. We dub this geometry the Hilbert-Killing metric, which allows us to study the onset of ergodicity in many-body quantum systems. Our Hilbert-Killing metric sensitively probes the boundary between ergodic and integrable regimes across all investigated geometric components. This boundary is uniquely identified by the presence of the consistently fastest growth with system size, which is corroborated by extensive numerical investigations of the Ising and PXP models.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper analyzes the anyon-Hubbard model to understand how fractional statistics influence quantum state complexity. Using Krylov complexity, the authors show that while scarred dynamics exhibit phase-independent revivals, quench dynamics are highly sensitive to the statistical phase and interaction strength. This highlights the central role of exotic statistics in governing many-body non-equilibrium behavior.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a sophisticated tool (Krylov complexity) to probe non-equilibrium dynamics in systems with exotic statistics, linking topological properties (anyons) directly to quantum information measures of complexity.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work investigates how anyonic statistics govern quantum-state complexity by studying the interplay between statistical phase and on-site interactions in the anyon-Hubbard model.

**Main result.** Krylov complexity shows perfect periodic revivals during scarred dynamics, but its behavior after a quench depends critically on both the initial and final statistical phases and interaction strength.

**Method.** The study employs Krylov complexity analysis ($C_K(t)$) and entanglement entropy ($S_A$) to characterize state spreading and distinguish between thermal and scar states in time evolution.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by the one-dimensional anyon-Hubbard model, characterized by a Hamiltonian involving hopping terms and an on-site interaction $U$, with statistical phase $	heta$ governing particle statistics (bosonic, fermionic, or fractional).

**Key observables.** Krylov Complexity ($C_K(t)$), Entanglement Entropy ($S_A$), Fidelity ($F(t)$), and the saturation plateau value of complexity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Statistical phase ($	heta$), on-site interaction strength ($U$), hopping amplitude ($J$), and system size ($L$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis involves constructing exact many-body scar eigenstates and analyzing dynamics in different regimes (strong vs. weak interaction).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the scaling of entanglement entropy for thermal versus scar states, and show time evolution plots of $C_K(t)$ confirming perfect revivals or saturation depending on quench parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the anyon-Hubbard model and its Hamiltonian. It then develops diagnostics like Krylov complexity and scar state construction. Key results are presented by analyzing dynamics under different conditions, such as no quench vs. quench, and varying interaction strengths.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Anyons obey fractional statistics that lie between bosonic and fermionic statistics, giving rise to a broad range of intriguing phenomena. However, how anyonic statistics govern quantum-state complexity is still largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate the interplay between the statistical phase and on-site interactions in the anyon-Hubbard model, identifying exact quantum many-body scar eigenstates and novel quench dynamics. The Krylov complexity exhibits perfect periodic revivals independent of the statistical phase in the scarred dynamics, whereas after a quench it depends on both the statistical phase and the interaction strength. In the strong-interaction regime, we find approximate scarred dynamics, while in the weak-interaction regime the state spreads over Krylov space and the complexity ultimately saturates. Moreover, for the bosonic initial state, the complexity of fermions exhibits the lowest saturation value, and vice versa. For fractional statistics, the saturation plateau is minimized when the post-quench statistical phase is close to that of the initial state. Our results demonstrate the central role of the statistical phase in governing many-body dynamics and provide new insights into Krylov complexity and quantum many-body scars.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors apply Restricted Boltzmann Machines within a Variational Monte Carlo framework to study a non-Hermitian Ising chain. They successfully map out a longitudinal-field-driven quantum phase transition characterized by spontaneous PT-symmetry breaking and magnetic ordering. This establishes RBMs as an efficient tool for analyzing critical phenomena in complex, interacting open quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work demonstrates a powerful, scalable numerical technique (RBMs) to analyze complex non-Hermitian dynamics, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems where gain/loss mechanisms are present.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Investigating the ground-state properties and quantum critical behavior of a non-Hermitian transverse-field Ising chain subjected to longitudinal and complex transverse magnetic fields.

**Main result.** The RBM approach successfully characterizes the PT-symmetry-breaking transition and the emergence of magnetic order in this challenging, interacting non-Hermitian system.

**Method.** The study employs real-valued neural quantum states (NQSs) based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), optimized using Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) sampling to tackle the many-body problem.

**Model / system.** The model is a 1D non-Hermitian Transverse-Field Ising Chain governed by a Hamiltonian incorporating transverse, longitudinal ($h$), and complex transverse fields ($\xi$). The system becomes non-integrable due to the longitudinal field.

**Key observables.** Ground-state energy (real part), magnetization ($M_z$), spin-spin correlation function ($C_{zz}(r)$), and detection of exceptional points (EPs).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Longitudinal field strength ($h$) and the imaginary transverse field parameter ($\xi$). Critical transition occurs around $h_c \approx 0.3$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The use of RBMs as a variational ansatz to approximate the ground state, which is necessary because exact diagonalization fails for large systems.

**Figures summary.** Figures show energy spectra revealing exceptional points (EPs) and track the evolution of the ground-state energy and magnetization across varying longitudinal fields ($h$), confirming phase transitions.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the Hamiltonian, develops the RBM-VMC framework for non-Hermitian systems, benchmarks results against ED, and then maps out quantum phase transitions by tracking symmetry breaking (PT) and magnetic order using multiple observables like $C_{zz}(r)$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the ground-state properties and quantum critical behavior of a non-Hermitian transverse-field Ising chain subjected to longitudinal and complex transverse magnetic fields. To address this interacting many-body problem, we employ real-valued neural quantum states based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), optimized using Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) sampling. Spectral analysis of finite chains reveals exceptional points associated with spontaneous parity-time (PT) symmetry breaking. A real-valued RBM framework is developed to reconstruct the ground-state eigenstates of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. Benchmark comparisons with exact diagonalization demonstrate that the RBM approach accurately reproduces the ground-state energy, magnetization, and spin-spin correlations. Extending the analysis to larger system sizes, we identify a non-Hermitian quantum phase transition characterized by PT-symmetry breaking and the emergence of magnetic order. Our results establish real-valued neural quantum states as an efficient and scalable framework for investigating critical phenomena in interacting non-Hermitian quantum systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces Conditional-Path Monte Carlo (CPMC), an advanced simulation technique designed to overcome the severe inefficiencies of standard methods when studying rare events in stochastic network dynamics. By performing non-local updates across entire spacetime clusters, CPMC accurately samples trajectories that satisfy complex macroscopic constraints without suffering from vanishing acceptance rates. This provides a powerful tool for analyzing critical risk factors in fields ranging from epidemiology to finance.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical stochastic processes, the methodology draws explicit inspiration from loop algorithms used in quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) for equilibrium physics. The development of a non-local update scheme that bypasses rejection sampling is highly relevant to simulating complex dynamics in many-body or open quantum systems where rare transitions are key.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central challenge is efficiently simulating stochastic evolution in complex networks when investigating rare macroscopic events, such as large-scale epidemic outbreaks or cascading failures.

**Main result.** The proposed Conditional-Path Monte Carlo (CPMC) method successfully generates trajectories respecting hard macroscopic boundary conditions without suffering from the catastrophic rejection rates or critical slowing down inherent to standard simulation techniques.

**Method.** CPMC is a novel rare-event sampling technique inspired by loop algorithms, employing non-local updates on spacetime clusters of the entire trajectory rather than step-by-step local integration.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on stochastic dynamics modeled using the Susceptible-Infectious-Susceptible (SIS) model applied to complex network structures, such as kinship networks. The general framework applies to any system exhibiting rare, constrained macroscopic transitions.

**Key observables.** Macroscopic boundary conditions (e.g., minimum outbreak size $N_{I}^{\min}$), conditional probabilities like the probability of being patient zero ($p_0^i$), and mean infection counts $\langle N_I(t) angle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Infection rate ($\alpha$) relative to recovery/removal rates, network structure metrics like closeness centrality ($c_i$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes that the trajectory can be mapped effectively onto an intermediate graph configuration $g$ using Swendsen-Wang-like updates for cluster identification.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 motivates the work by showing rare, large outbreaks on a contact network. Figure 2 illustrates the core mechanism: mapping a trajectory $\sigma$ to a compatible graph $g$ and identifying spacetime clusters $\{C_k\}$. Figure 3 analyzes risk factors using centrality measures. Figure 4 compares mean infection counts from CPMC against standard SSA simulations.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical problem (rare events in networks) and critiques existing methods (Gillespie, TPS, etc.). It then introduces the theoretical framework of CPMC, detailing its non-local cluster updates. The bulk of the work applies this method to the SIS model on real-world networks, validating it by comparing results against known simulations and performing risk factor analysis.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Understanding the stochastic evolution in complex networks is a central challenge across physics, biology, engineering, social science, and finance. The most consequential macroscopic events, like cascading failures in communication networks, widespread epidemic outbreaks, and rapid shifts in societal opinions, often emerge from a confluence of rare, localized stochastic processes and need to pass certain bottlenecks. Standard forward-time simulation algorithms like the Gillespie method are inefficient for the investigation of such phenomena due to catastrophic rejection rates. Advanced rare-event techniques like splitting methods and transition-path sampling often suffer from kinetic trapping, path degeneracy, genealogical correlations, or critical slowing down when applied to complex heterogeneous networks. We propose to overcome this challenge by establishing a novel technique called conditional-path Monte Carlo (CPMC), inspired by loop algorithms from equilibrium condensed-matter physics. By employing non-local updates on spacetime clusters without rejections, CPMC generates a Markov chain of trajectories that all strictly respect the targeted macroscopic boundary conditions like the occurrence of a massive network failure. We demonstrate the framework's potential by performing a simple risk factor analysis for rare large-scale epidemic outbreaks in SIS dynamics on kinship networks.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper explores tunable statistics-induced caging in the Anyon-Hubbard Model by applying Floquet engineering. It shows that while intrinsic interactions can cause caging only under specific conditions (strong coupling), external high-frequency driving can dynamically restore this effect even when interactions are weak. This provides a powerful tool for selectively controlling anyonic behavior based on their underlying statistical phase.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses coherent control of quantum many-body states using time-periodic driving, a central theme in AMO physics and open quantum systems research.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how quantum statistics can induce a controllable 'caging' effect for interacting anyons within the Anyon-Hubbard Model.

**Main result.** Dynamical control via Floquet engineering allows the restoration of this caging effect into the weakly interacting regime, enabling selective manipulation based on the statistical phase ($\kappa$).

**Method.** The analysis employs mapping to a Bose-Hubbard model and utilizes high-frequency expansion methods (Floquet theory) combined with perturbation theory to derive effective Hamiltonians.

**Model / system.** The system is the Anyon-Hubbard Model on a four-site plaquette, which is exactly mapped to a Bose-Hubbard type Hamiltonian. The dynamics are governed by time-dependent Schrödinger equations solved via Floquet engineering techniques.

**Key observables.** Target site occupation $\langle \hat{n}_3(t) angle$ and its long-time average $\langle \hat{n}_3 angle$, which quantifies the degree of caging (suppression to zero).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Statistical phase ($\kappa$), hopping amplitude ($J$), interaction strength ($U$), and external drive parameters (amplitude $A$, frequency $\omega$, polarization angle $	heta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on mapping the anyonic system to a bosonic model and employing high-frequency approximations for the time evolution.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the suppression of site occupation ($\langle \hat{n}_3 angle$) showing caging at specific parameter points, comparing results from effective Hamiltonians against full time-dependent simulations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing static caging in the strong interaction limit, then demonstrating its breakdown in weak coupling. The core contribution involves using Floquet engineering to dynamically restore this caging across all statistical regimes via an effective Hamiltonian approach.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the quantum dynamics of two interacting anyons in the Anyon-Hubbard model on a four-site plaquette, a system that is exactly mappable to a Bose-Hubbard model. We reveal that static Aharonov-Bohm (AB) caging, induced by only specific statistical phases, emerges in the strongly interacting limit but breaks down under weak interparticle interactions. To address this, we demonstrate that statistical-factor-induced AB caging can be dynamically restored via Floquet engineering. This dynamical mechanism, governed by the synthetic Floquet flux and the anyonic statistical phase, extends the caging effect into the weakly interacting regime across the full spectrum of statistical phases. Furthermore, we show that the external drive enables the selective caging of anyons, providing an efficient approach for manipulating anyons and identifying statistical phases.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces High-Dimensional Quantum Overlapping Tomography (QOT) to overcome the measurement complexity barrier in characterizing large, high-dimensional quantum states. Experimentally realized with photons, it efficiently reconstructs crucial two-body marginals using far fewer measurements than standard methods. The findings establish a scalable framework and demonstrate that this approach offers superior noise resilience for certifying multipartite entanglement.

**Why it may be interesting.** The development of scalable tomography techniques is crucial for validating quantum network components and understanding complex multi-partite correlations in high-dimensional photonic systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Characterizing large-scale, high-dimensional multipartite quantum systems is computationally prohibitive due to increasing local dimensionality and particle number.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated a scalable technique using High-Dimensional Quantum Overlapping Tomography (QOT) that reconstructs all two-body marginals with significantly fewer measurements than independent tomography. Furthermore, they showed this method provides more noise-resilient entanglement certification than fidelity-based criteria.

**Method.** They propose and experimentally implement QOT based on a graph-theoretic formulation, utilizing mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) to efficiently cover the necessary measurement settings required for marginal reconstruction.

**Model / system.** The experiment was performed on a photonic four-party entangled state in a $4 	imes 4 	imes 2 	imes 2$ system. The theoretical framework applies to general multipartite high-dimensional quantum systems.

**Key observables.** Two-body marginals ($ho_{XY}$), reconstruction fidelity ($0.876 \pm 0.014$), negativity, and global-to-local overlap ratios ($S$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of measurement settings required (25 vs. 94/225 for full tomography); the noise parameter $p$ used in simulating white noise contamination.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theoretical formulation is simplified for prime-power dimensions and relies on MUB measurements; entanglement certification comparisons assume a depolarizing channel model.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup using photonics, schematics of the underlying complete multipartite graph, reconstructed marginals (real parts, fidelities, negativities), and a comparison of entanglement criteria under noise.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of high-dimensional characterization, details the graph-theoretic QOT approach, presents the experimental realization on photonic states using MUB measurements, analyzes the reconstructed marginals for structure (e.g., layered entanglement), and concludes by comparing different entanglement certification methods under noise.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Large-scale quantum systems have advanced rapidly via the exploration of more particles and higher dimensions, offering great potential for developing quantum technologies. However, their characterization becomes prohibitive with increasing local dimensionality and particle number. Here we propose high-dimensional quantum overlapping tomography based on a graph-theoretic formulation, which allows one to efficiently reconstruct few-body marginals of multipartite high-dimensional quantum systems. We experimentally realize it on a photonic four-party entangled state in a $4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 2$ system. Using measurements in mutually unbiased bases, we reconstruct all six two-body marginals with only 25 projective measurement settings, compared with 94 and 225 settings for independent tomography of all two-body reduced states and full state tomography, respectively. The reconstructed marginals reveal a layered entanglement structure vital for high-dimensional quantum networks. We further show that these marginals enable more noise-resilient certification of multipartite high-dimensional entanglement than the fidelity-based criterion. Our work thus offers a scalable route for learning multidimensional quantum systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces Kraus-Parameterized Belief Reinforcement Learning for controlling open quantum systems based only on noisy measurements. By constraining the learned belief state ($\hat{ho}_t$) to maintain physical validity (PSD and trace normalization), the method ensures reliable control policies. This approach proves more stable than standard deep learning baselines, particularly when system dynamics change unexpectedly.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the practical implementation gap in quantum control theory by embedding fundamental physical constraints (like PSD) into the learning architecture, making RL policies applicable to real-world open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is achieving continuous quantum feedback control when only noisy measurement records are available, without direct access to the true underlying quantum state.

**Main result.** The proposed Kraus-Belief PPO method achieves stable feedback control with significantly lower return variance than unconstrained baselines, especially under out-of-distribution conditions.

**Method.** It uses a two-stage pipeline: a Kraus-constrained recurrent encoder estimates the density matrix ($\hat{ho}_t$), which is then fed into a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) actor for action selection.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a continuously monitored open quantum qubit, whose dynamics are governed by a stochastic master equation. Control involves applying a continuous scalar field $u_t$ to steer the state towards a target pure state $ho^\star$.

**Key observables.** Measurement-conditioned belief fidelity ($\sim 0.77–0.80$), return variance, mean episodic return, and physical validity metrics (PSD check, trace error).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Control action bounds ($u_t \in [-4, 4]$), measurement efficiency ($\eta$), and the PPO hyperparameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that enforcing physics-informed neural memory via the Kraus constraint acts as a practical inductive bias for reliable quantum feedback control.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the comparison between the Kraus-belief PPO pipeline and the LSTM baseline, highlighting how the Stiefel manifold projection enforces physical state constraints.

**Paper structure.** The paper defines the problem in terms of a POMDP, proposes the two-stage Kraus-Belief PPO method (encoder pretraining followed by RL control), compares it against an unconstrained LSTM baseline across nominal and OOD conditions, and analyzes performance metrics like variance stability.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum feedback control requires acting on noisy continuous measurement records without direct access to the underlying quantum state. We propose Kraus-Parameterized Belief Reinforcement Learning, a pipeline in which a recurrent encoder, constrained to the Stiefel manifold, produces density-matrix estimates that are guaranteed positive-semidefinite and trace-normalized by construction, embedding quantum state geometry directly into the learning loop. A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) actor then maps these physically valid belief states to continuous control actions. On a simulated continuously monitored qubit, the resulting policy achieves stable feedback control, maintaining a measurement-conditioned belief fidelity of approximately 0.77-0.80 and exhibiting substantially lower return variance than a parameter-matched LSTM-history baseline across both nominal and out-of-distribution conditions. Although gains in raw target fidelity are modest, the geometric constraint guarantees a physically valid, interpretable belief representation and yields markedly more stable control under measurement inefficiency and abrupt dynamics switches. These results indicate that physics-informed neural memory is a practical inductive bias for reliable quantum feedback control.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes how quantum information changes during local decoherence by examining quasiprobability trajectories. It demonstrates that these distributions can exhibit negative weights, leading to violations of certain mathematical criteria (Horváth's criterion). This highlights a fundamental difference between the full quantum trajectory description and what is observable only through average measurements.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, trajectory-level diagnostic tool that distinguishes quantum dynamics from classical stochastic processes, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems beyond simple average measurements.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates negative quasiprobability trajectories for Bell-diagonal quantum states undergoing local decoherence, contrasting trajectory-level dynamics with average-level inequalities.

**Main result.** Negative quasiprobabilities can violate Horváth's criterion for the Jensen-Steffensen inequality to hold, revealing a unique feature of quantum information dynamics invisible when only average quantities are considered.

**Method.** The authors use quasiprobability trajectories (Kirkwood-Dirac distribution) derived from fluctuation theorems applied to quantum mutual information change ($\Delta I$).

**Model / system.** The system consists of two qubits initialized in Bell-diagonal states and subjected to local decoherence channels, including dephasing, depolarizing, and amplitude damping.

**Key observables.** Quantum Mutual Information change ($\Delta I$), stochastic mutual information change ($\Delta\iota[\gamma]$), and the negativity of the quasiprobability distribution $Q[	ilde{\gamma}]$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Decoherence parameters such as $\lambda$ (dephasing) or $\eta$ (depolarizing noise); the analysis also depends on initial state populations ($p_k$) and environmental coupling strengths ($\mu$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The use of the Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution is necessary because spectral projectors for global and local states do not commute due to entanglement.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates that for initial Bell-diagonal states under dephasing or depolarization, the reduced trajectory weights $Q_S[\gamma]$ remain non-negative relative to the zero line.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the framework using fluctuation theorems and quasiprobabilities. It then analyzes specific decoherence channels (dephasing/depolarizing) showing non-negativity in reduced distributions, before focusing on amplitude damping to analytically determine minimum support values and prove the violation of Horváth's criterion.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The fluctuation theorem (FT) relates microscopic trajectory distributions to macroscopic averages. Using quasiprobability trajectories, this framework has recently been extended to quantum information dynamics. Despite sharing the form of conventional thermodynamic FTs, information FTs involve quasiprobabilities whose negativity and statistical properties remain poorly understood. We analytically determine the properties of negative distributions based on the two-qubit Bell-diagonal states evolving under local dephasing, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping channels. We show that the occurrence of negative quasiprobabilities is not determined by the entanglement or Bell nonlocality of the initial state. Instead, a diagonal-interference decomposition of the transition quasiprobability provides a sufficient condition for negativity. More importantly, we prove that quasiprobability distributions containing negative weights can violate Horváth's necessary and sufficient criterion for the Jensen-Steffensen inequality to hold for every continuous convex function, even though the specific exponential Jensen-like relation enforced by the FT and the quantum data-processing inequality remains valid. This trajectory-level contrast with classical stochastic descriptions reveals a distinctive feature of quantum information dynamics that is invisible when only the corresponding average-level information inequalities are considered.

</details>

**Summary.** The research tackles charge noise broadening in silicon T-centers, a major hurdle for quantum networking. By implementing an above-band optical pulse sequence, the authors successfully reset the local charge environment, dramatically narrowing the spectral linewidth. This demonstrates a robust, scalable method to create high-quality quantum emitters for integrated photonic circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses a critical bottleneck in solid-state quantum photonics by providing an active method to suppress spectral diffusion noise, which is crucial for scaling up quantum interconnects based on spin-photon interfaces.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The optical linewidth of single T-centers in silicon waveguides is broadened by fluctuating charge environments, which severely limits their use for high-fidelity quantum networking.

**Main result.** Above-band illumination provides an unheralded method to reset the local charge environment, narrowing the median linewidth by up to 3.5 times and achieving a narrowest reported linewidth of 128 MHz.

**Method.** The authors characterized the charge environment using pulsed photoluminescence excitation (PLE) measurements combined with electrical biasing and optical resetting techniques.

**Model / system.** The system involves single T-centers embedded in lateral p-i-n waveguides on silicon. The analysis models the measured spectral lineshape by decomposing the effective field into a deterministic external field ($E_{ext}$) and Gaussian charge noise ($\sigma_E$).

**Key observables.** Optical linewidth (FWHM), Rabi oscillation coherence time, local electric field shift (Stark effect), and charge-noise width ($\sigma_E$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Base temperature of 15 mK; initial linewidths in the GHz range; final narrowest linewidth of 128 MHz.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the measured lineshape can be modeled by averaging a Lorentzian over the charge noise distribution, and that the T-center transition frequency follows a quadratic Stark map.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate device schematics, pulse sequences (PLE/AB-PLE), voltage-resolved PLE spectrograms showing linewidth narrowing upon AB reset, and time-resolved measurements tracking charge environment recovery dynamics.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the problem (charge noise limiting indistinguishability) to presenting the novel measurement technique (AB-PLE resetting), quantifying the improvement across many emitters, and finally validating the underlying physics using Stark shift tuning and analytical modeling of the local field.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The silicon T-center is a telecom-band spin-photon interface in a manufacturable photonics platform. In nanophotonic devices, however, its optical linewidth is broadened by a fluctuating charge environment, limiting photon indistinguishability for quantum networking. Here, we address this challenge through characterization and suppression of the local charge-noise of single T-centers in lateral p-i-n waveguides, demonstrating an unheralded method of T-center optical linewidth narrowing. Above-band illumination resets the charge environment, neutralizing the local field and suppressing spectral diffusion. Across 46 emitters this reset narrows the median linewidth 3.5-fold to 0.57(11) GHz, and an optimized emitter reaches 128(22) MHz, the narrowest unheralded linewidth reported for an integrated T-center. The narrowed transition supports coherent optical Rabi oscillations with a coherence time of 20(2) ns. Finally, we perform Stark-shift tuning using the p-i-n junction, and read out the local electric field and the charge-noise width at 15 mK. An analytical model of proximal surfaces, bulk, and junction field effects provides good agreement with our findings. Our multi-pronged characterization of the nanophotonic-integrated T-center charge environment enables future device optimization toward scalable quantum interconnects.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports an experimental demonstration achieving high-throughput operation in a neutral-atom quantum processor by implementing non-destructive readout and atom reuse techniques. By integrating a photonic chip interface, the authors surpassed previous limitations to achieve a post-selected circuit iteration rate of 74.8 Hz. This work establishes a practical pathway toward building scalable, fast quantum computing hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses a critical engineering hurdle in quantum computing—the speed of operations. The focus on throughput optimization via resource management (atom reuse) is highly relevant for scaling up any physical qubit modality.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The practical performance of neutral-atom quantum processors is limited by low quantum circuit iteration rates (qCIRs) and overall information throughput.

**Main result.** The authors achieved a post-selected qCIR of 74.8 Hz, significantly improving throughput via an optimized methodology that utilized non-destructive readout and atom reuse.

**Method.** They implemented a high-throughput system using a chip-based photonic interface to enable fast, state-resolved, non-destructive readout and designed a benchmark sequence incorporating atom reuse between circuits.

**Model / system.** The platform is a neutral-atom array (using ${}^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms) integrated with an optical channel mapping (OCM) chip for parallel site-resolved readout. The core innovation lies in the ability to rapidly cycle qubits without full reloading.

**Key observables.** Raw qCIR (101 Hz), post-selected qCIR (74.8 Hz), and normalized Fisher information rate (57.7 Hz).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Retention probability of 99.7%; the cycle time is dominated by a $7	ext{ms}$ benchmark cycle.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The improvement relies on establishing a direct qubit-to-detector correspondence via the OCM chip, enabling non-destructive and fast readout.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup using the photonic chip (Fig. 1), detail the atom reuse benchmark sequence (Fig. 2), and show trade-offs between fidelity/retention probability versus readout duration (Fig. 2(d)).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first identifying the throughput bottleneck, then detailing the OCM chip integration for non-destructive readout, demonstrating the atom reuse protocol to achieve high raw qCIRs, and finally optimizing performance using the Fisher information rate.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Neutral-atom quantum processors have rapidly advanced in scale and coherence, yet their practical performance remains constrained by limited quantum circuit iteration rates (qCIRs) and information throughput. Here we experimentally demonstrate a high-throughput neutral-atom system based on non-destructive readout and atom reuse. By integrating a chip-based photonic interface with a 10-qubit array, we implement non-destructive readout with a retention probability of 99.7%, and further achieve a raw qCIR of 101Hz and a post-selected qCIR of 74.8Hz. More importantly, we verify a general throughput optimization methodology and obtain a normalized Fisher information rate of 57.7Hz, improving the achievable throughput by more than one order of magnitude compared with conventional methods. Our results establish a practical route toward high-throughput neutral-atom quantum processors.

</details>

**Summary.** The research overcomes the limitation of cycle-averaging in quantum light measurements by employing sub-cycle resolution metrology on bright squeezed vacuum. This technique reveals that the quantum state consists of stochastic, time-localized bursts whose relative phases are randomly distributed between two values separated by $\pi$. These random phase flips are then harnessed to generate high-rate quantum random number sequences approaching petahertz frequencies.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly bridges advanced quantum optics metrology (attosecond techniques) with quantum information processing by providing a physical mechanism to generate certified random numbers at extremely high bandwidths.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To measure the electric-field evolution of quantum light (femtosecond bright squeezed vacuum) with sub-cycle precision, overcoming limitations where conventional measurements average over multiple field cycles.

**Main result.** The study successfully characterized stochastic, time-localized bursts in the BSV and demonstrated that the random phase flips between adjacent bursts can be exploited to generate quantum random bit sequences at petahertz frequencies.

**Method.** Attosecond metrology techniques are adapted using nonlinear absorption on a silicon CMOS sensor to map the electric field $E(t)$ with sub-cycle resolution, followed by statistical analysis of phase differences.

**Model / system.** The system uses Bright Squeezed Vacuum (BSV) generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. The temporal structure is modeled using Whittaker–Shannon time-limited modes, which are localized in time and distinct from conventional Schmidt modes.

**Key observables.** Time-resolved coherence functions ($g^{(1)}(t_1, t_2)$, $g^{(2)}(t_1, t_2)$), burst statistics (number, duration), and the bimodal distribution of relative phase differences ($\Delta\phi$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Sub-cycle precision; petahertz generation rates; femtosecond burst widths ($\sim 17$ fs); $\pi$-separated phases.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The random phase flips are assumed to reflect spontaneous symmetry breaking, and the analysis relies on fitting procedures derived from theoretical models of joint spectral amplitudes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate experimental setups (Fig. 1a), pulse energy/signal histograms (Figs. 1b, 1c), representative burst waveforms (Fig. 1d), coherence function measurements (Fig. 4a/c), and the final NIST test results for randomness (Fig. S10).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from describing the fundamental limitation of cycle-averaged quantum optics to detailing the experimental measurement technique, characterizing the stochastic burst structure, and finally demonstrating the application of phase randomness for high-rate QRNG.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In quantum optics, quantization of the electromagnetic field typically occurs in a finite volume - a cavity - which results in discrete frequency modes where photons are created, annihilated and exchanged between such modes. As a result, evolution of quantum optical states is periodic in the carrier wave of the field, measurement protocols return cycle-averaged information, and any sub-cycle evolution that is foundational to many light-matter interactions, especially at high field strengths, remains hidden. Adapting an attosecond technique, here we capture the electric-field evolution of a quantum optical state, femtosecond bright squeezed vacuum, with sub-cycle precision. We find that it consists of many stochastic, time-localized bursts within each pump pulse whose phase randomly switches between two values. We exploit the random phase flips to generate quantum random bit sequences with a generation rate that can reach petahertz frequencies. In addition, the sub-cycle resolution allows us to measure coherence functions of the waveforms between any two times, which we explain with a superposition of time-limited modes. These results bridge attosecond metrology and quantum optics and pave the way to measuring quantum light-matter interactions as they evolve on a few-femtosecond time scale, and integrate quantum randomness in petahertz electronics.

</details>

<figcaption class="paper-figure-caption"><b>Fig 1.</b> FIG. 1. Deterministic adaptive execution in the TIDE quantum-control stack. An experiment compiler supplies the resident program, while decoder, estimator, or host logic provides runtime updates after execution begins. Within TIDE, parameter and instruction states associated with future operations remain revisable before the corresponding capture or fetch-visibility boundary. Complete event descriptors that cross the commitment boundary enter an independent hardware-timed dispatch path. **Summary.** The paper introduces TIDE, an FPGA processor designed for quantum control that enables adaptive execution by allowing runtime modification of future instructions and parameters. It achieves this determinism by strictly separating the revisable program state from a hardware-timed FIFO queue of committed events. This breakthrough allows complex, measurement-driven quantum experiments to be programmed reliably in real time.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the critical bottleneck in scaling quantum computation: building classical control electronics fast enough to handle mid-circuit measurement feedback. The deterministic separation of concerns is vital for realizing fault-tolerant quantum algorithms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is designing quantum control programs that can adapt their future operations based on real-time measurement outcomes without disrupting the timing of events already committed to hardware execution.

**Main result.** TIDE successfully implements a processor architecture that allows runtime revision of both parameters and instruction structure while guaranteeing deterministic, immutable service for all previously committed quantum control events.

**Method.** The system uses an FPGA-based processor (TIDE) that separates the program's revisable future from a hardware-timed, committed event stream using specialized update mechanisms.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is TIDE, an FPGA quantum-control processor implemented on a Xilinx ZCU102. It features a control core and a Time-Deterministic Peripheral-Control (TDPC) engine that manages the immutable dispatch of committed events.

**Key observables.** Committed descriptors remaining unchanged under subsequent perturbations; successful execution of revised sequences via DIPU/DISO; timing margins measured in clock cycles (e.g., 4 cycles for DIPU).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Control core frequency (250 MHz) and timing/update domain frequency (425 MHz); the size of the revision window (L-word overwrite length).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system assumes that successful FIFO acceptance marks event commitment, making descriptors immutable; it also relies on statically allocated extension regions for structural overwrites.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the TIDE quantum-control stack, showing how runtime feedback revises the future while the committed timeline remains deterministic. Figure 2 details the architecture, showing data flow between components like the control core and TDPC FIFOs.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of measurement-responsive quantum control, presents the TIDE architecture which separates revision from commitment via DIPU (parameter patch) and DISO (structural overwrite), validates its timing performance on hardware, and demonstrates that committed events are protected from subsequent runtime updates.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Measurement-responsive quantum experiments require control programs that can revise future operations after execution has begun without disturbing events already committed to precise timing. We present Time-Deterministic and Instruction-Dynamic Execution (TIDE), an FPGA quantum-control processor that separates a runtime-revisable future from a hardware-timed committed-event stream. TIDE provides two complementary update paths: Dynamic Instruction Parameter Update (DIPU) applies a one-shot patch to the next matching event before parameter capture, while Dynamic Instruction Stream Overwrite (DISO) performs guarded replacement, logical deletion, and out-of-line insertion in future resident-program regions. Per-channel committed-event FIFOs isolate accepted descriptors from subsequent control-core and update activity. The implemented Xilinx ZCU102 design meets timing at 250 MHz for the control core and 425 MHz for the timing/update domain. With downstream ready, every tested descriptor committed at least one timing-domain cycle before its programmed timestamp was dispatched in the programmed cycle at the registered output interfaces. In separate post-commit tests, committed timestamps and payloads remained unchanged under the applied perturbations. The minimum all-success mapped DIPU margin was four 250 MHz control-domain cycles. Under continuous payload delivery, an L-word contiguous overwrite completed in L+5 update-domain cycles. Within the characterized guard-distance range, rejected DISO requests preserved the resident path, whereas all admitted replacement, deletion, and insertion transactions exercised here executed a complete revised sequence. TIDE therefore enables runtime adaptation of both parameters and instruction structure while preserving deterministic service of committed quantum-control events.

</details>

**Authors:** Avi Marchewka

**Summary.** This paper reinterprets the unidirectional current from the MS formalism as a proper Positive Operator Valued Measure (POVM) for measuring first arrival time. By enforcing mathematical consistency via the resolution of the identity, the authors derive the required spectral response function $\lambda(k)$. This work establishes a deep connection between the MS approach and Kijowski's established framework, providing a unified theoretical description of quantum arrival-time statistics.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous, operator-based framework (POVM) for calculating time-of-arrival probabilities, resolving ambiguities in older interpretations like hazard rates, which is crucial for understanding measurement processes in quantum dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the quantum time-of-arrival (TOA) problem, which lacks a universally accepted observable in quantum mechanics.

**Main result.** It establishes that the unidirectional current derived from the MS formulation can be rigorously interpreted as a Positive Operator Valued Measure (POVM), and this POVM structure is shown to mathematically match Kijowski's arrival-time distribution.

**Method.** The authors construct an arrival-time POVM by generalizing the MS unidirectional current using a spectral response function $\lambda(k)$ and enforcing the resolution of the identity condition for free particles.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on a one-dimensional free particle confined to the negative half-line ($x<0$) with a Dirichlet boundary condition at the detector location ($x=0$).

**Key observables.** Unidirectional first-arrival current ($J_{UD}(t)$), arrival-time POVM ($	ext{E}(\Delta)$), and Kijowski's arrival-time distribution ($\Pi_K(t)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The spectral response function $\lambda(k) = \pi/(4k)$, the free particle dispersion relation, and time $t$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a phenomenological detector model with a diagonal, phase-free spectral response ($\lambda(k)$), and relies on the free-particle Hamiltonian.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the path decomposition of Feynman paths relative to the detector boundary at $x=0$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the MS unidirectional current, then generalizes it by treating the detection parameter $\lambda$ as a spectral function $\lambda(k)$. It derives the POVM from normalization constraints and finally establishes the mathematical equivalence between this POVM and Kijowski's two-sided arrival-time distribution.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Detector-based first-arrival models and operator-based arrival-time observables provide two conceptually distinct approaches to the quantum time-of-arrival problem. Here we connect these approaches by using the positive unidirectional first-arrival current of Marchewka and Schuss (MS) as the basis for constructing a family of positive arrival-time operators and, after normalization, an arrival-time POVM. The first-arrival character is inherited from the dynamics with a Dirichlet boundary, while the detector response is introduced at the amplitude level through a non-negative spectral function $λ(k)$.   For a one-dimensional free particle, resolution of the identity uniquely selects $λ(k)=\fracπ{4k}$, yielding an arrival-time POVM. The normalized unidirectional current can therefore be interpreted as a generalized Born-rule probability density rather than as a hazard rate, as in the original MS formulation.   We further show that the normalized one-sided MS amplitude coincides, up to an irrelevant phase, with the corresponding momentum-sector amplitude in Kijowski's arrival-time distribution. Consequently, the two directional contributions in Kijowski's distribution can be reproduced by two first-arrival problems defined on opposite sides of the boundary. This establishes an equivalence between the resulting arrival-time statistics while emphasizing the different physical interpretations: MS describes a first-arrival process with coherent momentum components, whereas Kijowski's POVM treats the two momentum sectors as separate directional contributions.   Thus, the normalized unidirectional current provides a POVM description of first arrival at a point, combining detector-based dynamics with a positive-operator measurement structure.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a phase-space path-integral formalism to explain anomalous weak pointer shifts. It shows that these seemingly unusual shifts are mathematically equivalent to constructive interference among multiple coarse-grained quantum histories. This offers a powerful, intuitive picture of measurement outcomes while maintaining consistency with fundamental conservation laws in the full closed system.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a deep theoretical interpretation of weak measurements and pointer shifts within the framework of quantum histories, connecting non-classical measurement outcomes to fundamental concepts like interference and conservation laws in a path-integral setting.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper reformulates anomalous weak pointer shifts, which allow effective measurements outside an observable's eigenvalue range, by interpreting them as interference among coarse-grained histories.

**Main result.** The postselected momentum distribution behaves as if it were translated by an effective shift $\gamma A_w$, providing a path-integral representation of the anomalous weak value effect via history interference.

**Method.** The analysis uses phase-space path integrals, applying superoscillatory approximations to sum over branch-conditioned amplitudes derived from measurement coupling.

**Model / system.** The model involves a quantum system ($\hat{A}_s$) coupled weakly to a pointer observable ($\hat{x}_p$), analyzed using path integral techniques and focusing on the resulting momentum readout.

**Key observables.** Anomalous weak value ($A_w$), effective mean momentum shift $\langle p angle = p_i + \gamma A_w$, and the total conserved generator $Q_{	ext{tot}}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The coupling constant ($\gamma$) and the window size defining the superoscillatory approximation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on satisfying a finite superoscillatory-window condition for the initial momentum wavepacket, and it is explicitly noted not to be a complete resolution of all conservation law puzzles.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by introducing the anomalous shift, reformulating it in path integrals using branch conditioning, applying superoscillatory approximations to derive an effective momentum translation, and finally analyzing how this structure relates to symmetry constraints via Ward identities.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Anomalous weak values and superoscillations allow a pointer to exhibit an effective shift outside the eigenvalue range of the measured observable. We reformulate this effect in a phase-space path-integral language. For each eigenvalue branch $a_j$ of the measured observable, {the interaction couples $a_j$ to the pointer position $\hat{x}_p$ and thereby translates the conjugate pointer momentum by $γa_j$.} After postselection, {the branch-conditioned amplitudes are coherently superposed with coefficients chosen to produce a superoscillatory approximation. When this conditional amplitude acts on an initial pointer momentum wavepacket for which the finite superoscillatory-window condition is satisfied, the resulting momentum wavefunction behaves as if it had been translated by $γA_w$, rather than by any of the eigenvalue-conditioned shifts $γa_j$. This yields an effective path-integral representation of anomalous weak pointer shifts and motivates their interpretation in terms of interference among finite coarse-grained histories.} We discuss how this picture bears on conservation-law questions.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an architecture to enable hybrid High Performance Computing and Quantum Computing (HPCQC) workflows on large-scale supercomputers. It achieves this using a heterogeneous software stack that integrates the QPU into existing schedulers like SLURM by treating it as a managed accelerator. The successful demonstration proves that quantum resources can be incorporated with minimal performance overhead, paving the way for practical quantum acceleration in national labs.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on software infrastructure rather than fundamental physics, the work directly addresses the operationalization of quantum hardware by providing a robust, standardized interface layer necessary for any future experimental study in AMO or open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is integrating Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) into existing, established High Performance Computing (HPC) supercomputing workflows.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated hybrid HPCQC workflows on a production petascale system with negligible latency overhead compared to purely classical workloads.

**Method.** They developed and implemented a heterogeneous software stack featuring a two-level scheduling model orchestrated by an open-source SLURM Plugin Suite.

**Model / system.** The system combines the SuperMUC-NG supercomputer, a 20-qubit superconducting QPU from IQM, and the Munich Quantum Software Stack (MQSS). This architecture treats QPUs as scheduler-managed accelerators.

**Key observables.** Latency overhead for hybrid jobs, average circuit runtimes for QAOA/VQE benchmarks, and real-time QPU status metrics like fidelity and calibration status.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The system operates on a petascale scale, utilizing 20 superconducting qubits, and employs SLURM's GRES mechanism for resource reservation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The approach assumes that treating QPUs as scheduler-managed Generic Resources (GRES) is feasible without modifying the core scheduler logic. It also notes limitations regarding joint optimization of classical/quantum resources.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the MQSS architecture, detailing the flow from front-end adapters through the QRM&CI to the quantum device, and show job pipeline examples within SLURM context.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the necessity for integration, presents the two-level scheduling model (SLURM at Level 1, QRM&CI at Level 2), describes the implementation via plugins, and validates performance using benchmark measurements.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we demonstrate hybrid High Performance Computing-Quantum Computing (HPCQC) workflows on a production petascale system. The demonstration combines three components: the SuperMUC-NG supercomputer at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ), a 20-qubit superconducting quantum processor provided by IQM Quantum Computers (IQM), and Munich Quantum Valley (MQV)'s Munich Quantum Software Stack (MQSS).   Integrating quantum processors into High Performance Computing (HPC) systems requires a heterogeneous software stack capable of orchestrating classical and quantum resources within established supercomputing workflows. MQSS treats Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) as scheduler-managed accelerators and it performs resource coordination following a two-level scheduling scheme. Slurm performs system-level allocation by exposing QPUs as Generic RESources (GRES), while the MQSS Quantum Resource Manager & Compiler Infrastructure (QRM&CI) performs just-in-time compilation and subsequent dispatch of quantum circuits.   To integrate with existing HPC operations without modifying the scheduler core, MQSS introduces an open-source SLURM Plugin Suite based on Prolog/Epilog scripts and SPANK modules. Experimental results show that hybrid HPCQC workflows can be executed without significant latency overhead compared to conventional workloads.   The presented architecture provides a portable integration model for quantum accelerators on large-scale HPC systems and is directly applicable to next-generation Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Cray platforms, including LRZ's upcoming 'Blue Lion' supercomputer.

</details>

**Summary.** The researchers engineered two-qubit gates in germanium hole spin qubits by exploiting the anisotropic nature of the exchange interaction, which arises from strong spin-orbit coupling. By controlling the external magnetic field direction, they achieved continuous tuning of the exchange Hamiltonian, enabling novel gate operations like a baseband iSWAP. This work demonstrates how material physics can be leveraged for precise quantum control in solid-state quantum computing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete experimental realization of native Hamiltonian engineering in solid-state qubits, showing how material properties (g-tensors) dictate controllable quantum gates, which is highly relevant for building scalable quantum processors.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to engineer high-fidelity two-qubit quantum gates (like CPhase and iSWAP) by precisely controlling the anisotropic exchange interaction in germanium spin qubits.

**Main result.** They demonstrated continuous control over the exchange coupling Hamiltonian by reorienting the external magnetic field, achieving a single-pulse baseband iSWAP gate unattainable with isotropic coupling.

**Method.** The study uses state spectroscopy (ARP) and Quantum Process Tomography (QPT) to map out the energy spectrum and characterize the fidelity of implemented quantum gates.

**Model / system.** The platform is hole spin qubits in a strained-germanium quantum well. The interaction Hamiltonian is modeled as an anisotropic exchange tensor, decomposed into longitudinal ($J_{\|}$) and transverse ($J_{\perp}$) components, which are tunable by the magnetic field orientation ($\vec{B}$).

**Key observables.** CPhase oscillation frequency ($f_{C	ext{Phase}}$), SWAP-like oscillation frequency ($f_{	ext{SWAP}}$), coherence times ($T_2^*$, $T_H$), and process fidelity ($F_{	ext{iSWAP}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ability to tune the sign of the longitudinal exchange coupling ($J_{\|}$) from positive through zero to effectively negative is a key parameter control.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The fidelity estimate relies on assuming depolarizing error channels and ignoring coherent error components during the SPAM sequence analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate device structure, single-qubit g-tensors vs. B field, energy level diagrams showing $J_{\|}$ (Ising) and $J_{\perp}$ (XY) coupling, and measurements of gate fidelity via QPT/iSWAP characterization.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical system and Hamiltonian components derived from g-tensor anisotropy to measuring these couplings using spectroscopy, culminating in the demonstration and quantification of two-qubit gate fidelities.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Germanium hole spin qubits are a promising and versatile platform for quantum computation and simulation. In this system, strong spin-orbit interaction (SOI) renders the single-qubit $g$-tensor anisotropic and electrically tunable, enabling operational sweet spots with reduced noise sensitivity. SOI also transforms the isotropic two-qubit exchange coupling into an anisotropic tensor whose geometry is inherited from the single-qubit $g$-tensors and spin-flip tunnelling. Here, using two hole spin qubits in a strained-germanium quantum well and full vector control of the magnetic field, we map this exchange tensor, separate it into longitudinal and transverse components, and show that they govern controlled-phase and SWAP-like dynamics, respectively. We find that the longitudinal exchange can be tuned via the magnetic field orientation from a conventional positive value, through zero, to an effectively negative one, as measured by inverted exchange-split spin transitions. The magnetic field direction thus provides continuous control over the interaction Hamiltonian: at a point of purely transverse exchange, we engineer a single-pulse baseband iSWAP, unattainable under isotropic exchange. Linking $g$-tensor geometry to exchange anisotropy establishes native Hamiltonian engineering, enabling spin-based quantum simulation and gate sets selected by the global field orientation alone.

</details>

**Summary.** This work rigorously calculates the ultimate performance limit (minimax cost) for estimating an unknown qubit direction. It proves that the optimal measurement strategy must be Haar random and establishes a strict hierarchy showing how restricting measurements (e.g., to local operations) degrades achievable precision compared to ideal collective measurements.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous, quantitative bounds on quantum estimation precision, which is fundamental to understanding the limits of quantum sensing protocols in both theory and experimental realization.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the exact worst-direction Fisher-information cost for estimating an unknown qubit direction using a parameter-independent readout.

**Main result.** It proves that the optimal aggregate measurement design is uniquely the spin-coherent Haar POVM, and it establishes strict resource separation between different types of local measurements (e.g., fixed-local vs. collective).

**Method.** The analysis involves solving a minimax optimization problem by reducing the readout process to optimizing over zero-barycenter probability measures on the Bloch ball.

**Model / system.** The system is a qubit whose state is parameterized by an unknown direction $\mathbf{n}$ on the Bloch sphere $S^2$, with a known fixed length $\eta$. The measurement process involves comparing different readout architectures (fixed-local, LOCC, collective POVMs).

**Key observables.** Worst directional Fisher loss, A-loss coefficient, and the aggregate design measure $\mu$ on the Bloch ball.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Bloch-vector length $\eta$, number of copies $N$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes fixed-local architectures are equivalent to zero-barycenter probability measures, and it compares performance across various measurement constraints (LOCC vs. unrestricted).

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by establishing the equivalence between physical readout schemes and mathematical optimization over aggregate design measures, deriving explicit formulas for the minimax loss under different assumptions, and finally comparing these bounds to show resource separation.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We determine the exact worst-direction Fisher-information cost of using a parameter-independent readout to estimate an unknown qubit direction at known Bloch-vector length $η$. Every fixed-local architecture, including recorded classical randomization, heterogeneous single-copy measurements, and arbitrary outcome spaces, reduces exactly to a zero-barycenter probability measure on the Bloch ball. For every full-rank qubit and every trace-balanced spectral Fisher loss, the resulting minimax problem is rigid: the unique optimal aggregate design is the spin-coherent Haar positive-operator-valued measure (POVM). For $N$ copies, inverse-Fisher $A$ loss has the exact value $2/[Nf(η)]$, where $   f(η)=   \frac{2η-(1-η^2)\log[(1+η)/(1-η)]}{4η}$. This uniqueness has an immediate finite-readout consequence. No finite-support measurement attains the unrestricted mixed-state optimum, while at the smallest globally regular support the tetrahedral symmetric informationally complete (SIC) measurement is uniquely $A$- and $D$-minimax, with exact worst-direction values. Relaxing the fixed-readout constraint separates the asymptotic resources: one-way local operations and classical communication (LOCC), unrestricted LOCC, and separable measurements have $A$-loss coefficient $4/η^2$, whereas collective measurements attain $2(1+η)/η^2$. We further classify the rigidity conditions for unequal contrasts and show that Haar uniqueness survives at the nonregular pure-state endpoint.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes quantum computation using shallow circuits that incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward. It proves a strict hierarchy of computational power based on the amount of classical information fed back into the circuit. Crucially, it demonstrates that polynomial feedback allows these local measurements to solve classically hard problems like DLP, opening a new pathway for achieving quantum advantage with resource-efficient circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides concrete, resource-aware benchmarks for quantum advantage by showing how adaptive measurement feedback fundamentally changes the complexity landscape compared to static entanglement measures.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research addresses determining the minimal resource requirements for achieving quantum advantage when measurements are restricted to local observables rather than full state sampling.

**Main result.** Increasing the amount of classical feedback in adaptive shallow circuits strictly increases computational power, enabling the encoding of classically hard problems like DLP into a single local expectation value with polynomial feedback.

**Method.** The authors establish computational hierarchies by analyzing the class of functions accessible via local expectation values ($\langle O angle$) based on the complexity of the classical feedforward mechanism ($m$).

**Model / system.** The model is Adaptive Shallow Circuits (CRAS) featuring constant coherent depth layers interleaved with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward, culminating in a single fixed local observable measurement.

**Key observables.** Local expectation value ($\langle O angle$) of a fixed single-qubit observable; the required amount of classical feedback ($m$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The scaling of classical feedback $m$ (e.g., $O(\log n)$ vs. polynomial in $n$); computational depth ($d$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The hardness results are conditional on the standard worst-case classical hardness of the Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP).

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the transition from non-adaptive to adaptive circuits, showing how feedback enables global processing. Other figures detail the construction of complex gates like controlled rotations and Threshold gates on a 2D lattice.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the computational hierarchy using DLP hardness for local readout (Chunk 1 & 2). It then provides detailed constructions demonstrating that complex logical operations, including arithmetic circuits, can be implemented efficiently in terms of depth and rounds on a 2D nearest-neighbor architecture (Chunk 3 & 4).

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum advantage is widely expected to require sufficiently deep circuits, where correlations and global computational structure can grow beyond the reach of efficient classical simulation. This expectation is especially stark for constant-depth circuits with local readout: the expectation value of any fixed local observable lies within a bounded backward lightcone and is therefore classically tractable. Here we show that measurement feedback changes this picture. We establish a strict hierarchy of computational power: at fixed coherent depth, increasing the number of feedback outcomes strictly enlarges the class of functions accessible through a local expectation value. The two ends of this hierarchy exhibit distinct computational regimes. With logarithmic feedback, local expectation values for product-state inputs are efficiently classically simulable. Polynomial feedback, by contrast, enables an explicit family of adaptive shallow circuits to encode prime-field discrete logarithm problem~(DLP) into a fixed single-qubit expectation. Assuming the standard worst-case classical hardness of DLP, estimating this expectation value is classically hard. These results reveal a feedback-driven complexity transition, with further implications for resource lower bounds on DLP and the complexity of local-observable estimation under area-law entanglement. Our results open a new route to quantum advantage with shallow quantum circuits.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study models chiral nonlinear optics in waveguides using a two-level emitter coupled to multiple optical fields. By employing the Green's Tensor formalism, the authors show that chirality enables superior control over photon dynamics compared to symmetric setups. The results predict highly efficient all-optical switching and amplification crucial for quantum networking applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses quantum network protocols by demonstrating highly controllable, non-reciprocal nonlinear light-matter interactions necessary for advanced photonic quantum devices.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work investigates chiral nonlinear interactions between light (signal and control beams) and a quantum emitter in photonic waveguides to achieve all-optical control of photons.

**Main result.** Chiral geometries enable robust, tunable $0-\pi$ phase shifts and significantly enhance signal amplification ($\sim 100	imes$) compared to standard predictions.

**Method.** The authors develop a model using the Green's Tensor formalism and solve the emitter dynamics via the Lindblad master equation in the rotating frame.

**Model / system.** The system involves a two-level quantum emitter coupled to a waveguide, driven by both signal ($\omega_s$) and control ($\omega_c$) beams. The theory incorporates chirality through directional coupling parameters ($D$).

**Key observables.** Transmission ($T$), reflection ($R$), coherent transmission ($T_{	ext{coh}}$), and the phase shift of the transmitted signal beam.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Few-photon regime ($ar{n}_c < 1$), chirality parameter ($D$), detunings ($\delta$), and Rabi frequencies ($\Omega_{s/c}^R$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on time averaging to remove oscillatory terms, and approximations are used for calculating relative population contributions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the setup comparing symmetric vs. chiral coupling; spectra show TLE interaction signatures in $T$ and $R$; other figures compare normalized transmission under different control powers.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from first principles using a Green's Tensor formalism to model the Hamiltonian, derives equations of motion for the density matrix, calculates time-averaged observables like transmission, and finally compares results between symmetric and chiral geometries.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Chiral light-matter interactions lie at the heart of emerging technologies such as quantum network protocols and quantum logic gates. In the few photon regime, it has been shown that chiral interactions between photons and a waveguide-embedded two-level quantum emitter can break reciprocity and impart a directional $π$ phase shift while the transmission remains intact. In this work, we present a model for multicolor, chiral nonlinear interactions in waveguides using a Green's Tensor formalism. We challenge previously held notions and demonstrate the complex photon dynamics hidden in multicolor light-matter interactions in the few photon regime. By modulating a stronger control beam, we can manipulate a weaker signal beam that contains much less than a single photon per emitter lifetime, on average. We develop equations for the transmission of the signal photons and removing the control photons to uncover the true strength of these nonlinearities, which we show is stronger than what is possible in symmetric geometries. The model predicts tunable unity extinction and up to 30% amplification in the signal, a $\sim$100x increase from standard predictions in which control photons are present. We also predict a tunable 0-$π$ phase shift via control modulation with significant robustness to emitter imperfections. Our model opens a new regime of directional nonlinear quantum light-matter interactions for study, providing a route to efficient all-optical control of photons.

</details>
